To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the content of free (unbound), absorbable phenolic acids and antioxidant capacity of bread and bread hydrolysate significantly increased in comparison to the starting material, and that the fermentation type had no significant impact on the results.

the content of free (unbound, easily absorbable) phenolic acids in wholemeal bread and its hydrolysates is significantly higher than in flour and that the increase is the highest for rye samples, which is important for the potential use of wholemeal rye bread as a source of phenolic acids and antioxidants.

the fermentation of bread with baker's yeast or with baking starter made of S. chevalier, L. casei and L.brevis cultures increases the content of free (unbound, bioactive) phenolic acids, and consequently the antioxidant capacity of wholemeal wheat, spelt and rye breads and their in vitro hydrolysates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the changes in the free phenolic acids content of wholemeal breads during baking and in vitro digestion and their relation to the antioxidative capacity of these products.
the changes in the content of phenolic acids in wholemeal breads during the fermentation process, which can be a crucial factor for their bioavailability.
the impact of fermentation type on the content and antioxidative capacity in bread, as well as on their changes during in vitro bread hydrolysis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
fermentation of breads and their further processing by enzymatic hydrolysis can be used as a tool for increasing free phenolic acid levels in the final product.

the fermentation type and cereal species can affect the content of free (unbound, bioavailable) phenolic acids in wholemeal bread and their final bread hydrolysates, which can affect the final bread quality and health-promoting properties.

free phenolic acid contents of the studied breads and their in vitro hydrolysates increased during the fermentation, and that the antioxidative capacity of the final products is related to the phenolic acid profile.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fermentation type does not have a significant impact on the free phenolic acid concentration and antioxidant capacity of the bread, but it does have a significant impact in the hydrolysate.
fermentation of wholemeal flour can be used as a tool for increasing the antioxidative capacity of bread, especially in rye flour, which is rich in phenolic acids.
the fermentation type and cereal species have a significant effect on phenolic acid content and antioxidative capacity, but the final results are strongly affected by initial flour composition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the fermentation type has a significant impact on the free phenolic acids content in bread and their hydrolysate, and that this can be used to improve the health benefits of bread.
the increase of the phenolic acid content is a result of the fermentation process, but the increase in the antioxidative capacity is not always proportional to the increase in free phenols.
the content and antioxidative capacity can be increased in bread and its hydrolysate by using wholemeal rye flour and by the use of fermentation.
